articles.title: RIP Tom Skerritt: Read Our Archival Alien Interview With the Late Actor
articles.summary: On Alien's 40th anniversary, actor Tom Skerritt looks back at the classic film that he initially feared ‘could be an Ed Wood movie.’
articles.body:
With the news that actor Tom Skerritt has died at the age of 93, I thought readers might want to take a look at this interview that I did with him several years back where we did a deep dive into his memories of making Ridley Scott's classic Alien . Skerritt was so great as Captain Dallas in that film, the sort of beleagured boss type who has too much on his plate and too many assholes working for him. But the actor was also memorable in so many other projects, not the least of which was in Robert Altman's original M*A*S*H movie, as the sheriff in David Cronenberg's great The Dead Zone, as the lead on the TV series Picket Fences, and so much more.

Read on for that chat I had with him, unedited from its original form.

It was 40 years ago, on May 25, 1979, that audiences learned the meaning of the phrase "In space, no one can hear you scream." Ridley Scott’s classic horror/sci-fi hybrid Alien opened in theaters on that day, and genre cinema was changed forever as a result.

To celebrate the anniversary, IGN recently spoke with Tom Skerritt, who of course played Dallas in the film, the captain of the commercial towing vehicle Nostromo. Dallas is a working class guy who happens to do that work in space, and he finds himself up against much more than he bargained for when his crew, including of course Sigourney Weaver’s Ripley, inadvertently brings the xenomorph of the title onboard…

While Alien would prove to be one of the most important films in Skerritt’s career, he was initially reluctant to take on the project. He was the first actor among the cast to receive the script, even reading it before Ridley Scott was onboard. An indeed, it was Scott’s eventual involvement that would help change Skerritt’s mind about Alien.

“This one came along and I read it and I thought, ‘Well, it's okay. I mean, it's crafted well,’” he told IGN. “And they said, ‘You're the only one they sent it to. There's no director and no other actors and it's a $2 million budget.’ And I thought, ‘Hold on, a $2 million budget, no director… And it feels like it could be an Ed Wood movie!’”

Meanwhile, Skerritt had coincidentally seen Scott’s first feature The Duellists around this time.

“It just knocked me out,” he continued. “I thought, ‘Oh God, I'd love to mentor with this guy, watch him and see how he works.’ A couple of weeks later they called me up and said, ‘So the budget's been kicked up to $10 million and they found a director and it's a guy named Ridley Scott. And I said, ‘Sold. Sold!’ It's really from the beginnings always been about the directors in looking at material. And that's basically how that whole thing for me started with Alien.”

Once production got under way, the actor followed Scott around on set “like a little puppy.” He says he knew from the get-go that Alien was going to be something special.

“He was omnipotent on the whole set,” Skerritt said. “He would say, ‘Well for this effect, you'd use this lens here that I'm looking at. And now I'm going out.’ And he goes out and he moves some tapioca around on the [prop] head of Ian Holm. You've got the head sitting there and the tapioca sitting around there and he's just moving some of these things, these little objects on a table, toward the back so that you get a little more depth of field and a little enhancement over here and lighting. He would correct lighting because there was some effect he wanted. All this stuff he was sharing with me. … That one I felt, yes, we were making a classic. I knew that. I'd gone through that thing with [director] Bob Altman [on M*A*S*H] and recognized that this is something special. And that's how I felt about Alien very, very soon into it.”

One of the most interesting -- and surprising, especially in 1979 -- aspects of Alien is the subversion of expectations regarding Dallas. The audience is set up to expect Dallas to be the hero who's going to see us through to the end; he’s the traditional male lead who will defeat the monster. But Alien pulls the rug out from under us about three quarters of the way into the movie when Dallas is abruptly killed off, which of course opens things up for Weaver’s Ripley to take over.

“Yes, that was an appeal to me because, let's face it, us guys have egos,” he said. “I really don't have that. … And I said, ‘Great.’ I had done Turning Point, which was basically a woman's film and I just loved that women were getting some focus. Now, I wasn't familiar with Sigourney initially. All I knew was she was an up and coming, really good theater -- Broadway -- actor. Thinking in terms of whether it matters whether you played first fiddler or second fiddle, it's nice to be in a great orchestra.

Of course, there is the question of what the true relationship was between Ripley and Dallas. Onscreen, it’s strictly professional, with Dallas serving as Ripley’s captain. But in some of the book adaptations, it has been implied that either Dallas had feelings for Ripley or that there was a sexual relationship between the two. Skerritt said that while there was an implication of romance between the characters in the Alien script, they never shot any scenes to that effect.

“There was some innuendo there of her concern about his well-being and a little bit more of that,” said the actor. “But doing it, when you got into, you really felt that that's intrusive too. Where's that gonna go? You've got this monster and you have no idea where it is or what it is. [Ridley Scott] said he was going to not get into that for those reasons that it seems to have its own pace by itself. And if you have this little love affair going on, it detracts from that. It was too intense, we realized.”

Alien fans know that Dallas’ death in the theatrical cut of Alien is quite different from where he originally wound up when the film was shot. The Director’s Cut reveals that Dallas didn’t die in that air duct where the alien initially attacked him, but rather he was taken back to the Nostromo’s hold to be cocooned and slowly, horrifically turned into an alien egg. Ripley stumbles upon this scene and, with Dallas begging her to kill him, torches her captain to spare him this fate.

“It took a couple of days to really set all that up,” said Skerritt. “And at the time I remember talking with Ridley about that. I said, ‘Does doing this scene slow the pace down? Of her having to get herself off that plane now.’ We feel that. He says, ‘It might, but I want to have it just in case.’”

The actor wasn’t bothered that this scene was ultimately cut from the original version of the film.

“It didn't matter to me,” he laughed. “All I know is that he doesn't get to the end. That's all I knew at the time and it was going to be that way. It was going to be a woman's picture in the end. That just appealed to me.”

Scott was ahead of schedule at that point in production and “within the parameters” of the budget, so he built the set and took the time to shoot the scene even though he wasn’t sure if he’d use it.

“A little bit of latitude gives a great director, a little bit of experimentation about what you can and cannot do,” continued Skerritt. “And he was able to get what he needed for his own frame of reference out of that at no cost really, because he was already under budget and had some time that he could put into it. So you work with somebody like that, you indulge them. You can do nothing less than learn.”

Even if that means putting on a little bit of tapioca pudding and hanging on the wall for a couple of days.

“Oh yeah, that sounded terrible,” laughed Skerritt. “I'm just imagining the smell of it!”

Go watch Alien tonight and celebrate this classic.

Talk to Scott Collura @scottcollura.bsky.social , or listen to his Star Trek podcast, Transporter Room 3 . Or do both!

articles.title: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York Review - IGN
articles.summary: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York review: John Turturro keeps a dying criminal profession alive.
articles.body:
This review is based on a screening from the Sundance Film Festival. The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is in limited theatrical release beginning October 23 and goes wide October 30.

In The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, writer and director Noah Segan yearns for a bygone Big Apple. The film, set in modern times, is a jazzy, sentimental ode to the New York City of yesteryear; it's sappy and starry-eyed, but also tenderly humorous in bursts. At other times, the story becomes a sad glimpse into the lost art of pickpocketing – not that the production advocates for thievery, but Segan uses a slick aging swindler to reminisce about an American hub that's been digitized by tech magnates and overrun with nepotism babies.

John Turturro is magnificent as Harry, an old-school pickpocket who's keeping the outdated art form alive. He has to; it's the only way he can caretake for his non-responsive, invalid wife, Rosie (Karina Arroyave). One night, he swipes a wallet and gym bag from an especially prickish dudebro using only a penny; what he finds is a gun, wads of cash, and a doohickey that plugs into a computer. Harry trashes the gun and sells the credit-card-looking object with a USB plug, which turns out to be very, very important. Soon enough, thugs come looking for the revealed crypto key. Either Harry retrieves the stolen item, or he's facing harsh consequences.

Segan's maturation as a filmmaker from Blood Relatives to The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is like the difference between Staten Island and Manhattan; it's so intrinsically ‘New Yawk’ in both commemoration and adoration. There's a song-and-dance about Harry's remembrance of the good times, and spot-on comedy as Harry tries to catch up with civilization. Segan roasts the entitled youth who have brought their sour attitudes and pretension to the East Coast’s bustling metropolis, as he interacts with elder characters like Steve Buscemi’s pawn-star Ben about how no one's word means a damn anymore. At times, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York plays like a lively stoop conversation between neighborhood elders who've seen their block change over decades (a compliment).

Turturro is, as ever, a gift to audiences. His portrayal of Harry is that of a lovable hustler whose movements are smoother than butter. He's a man of the people, whether jawing about the golden days of pickpocketing with Detective Warren (Giancarlo Esposito) like retirement home buddies, or treating Rosie like a princess (carrying her up staircases, reading her corny romance novels). Turturro's slippery maneuvers sell Harry as this masterclassman of his illegal profession, but once he's in over his head, his desperation hits like a semi-truck. Is there any actor more charming, too suave, and yet vulnerable once the deck is stacked against him? If you need one more reason to classify Turturro as a multigenerational talent, it's The Only Living Pickpocket in New York.

As for the pickpocketry, Segan treats Harry's lifestyle like a dying art; either you adapt, or you fade away. Scores have dwindled because no one carries cash anymore – just trackable cards and smartphone wallets. Harry's execution is flawless, snatching wallets like he's invisible, wearing overcoats with tactical pockets to ensure the shortest path from removal to hiding spot. There's something romantic about the way Harry scoffs at the cyberthieves of younger generations – Victoria Moroles' whippersnapper Eve roasts the fogey right back – but mentors up-and-comers who need guidance. Weirdly enough, the death of pickpockets in New York signals this changing of the times, which Segan treats with warm reverence.

Segan and his team succeed in authentically recreating the nooks and crannies of New York City. Cinematographer Sam Levy squeezes the camera into the confined spaces of corner pawn shops, barren vape bodegas, and humble Bronx apartments while still capturing the city's grandness. Composer Gary Lionelli honors the jazz-esque tempo with which Harry operates by delivering a bouncy, fleet-of-foot score. Impressively, Segan's representation of New York, New York smacks of Woody Allen or Martin Scorsese; the way he navigates the one-of-a-kind sights and sounds evokes nostalgia for my years in Brooklyn, a testament to the connection Segan strikes with the city.

Plain and simple, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York features veteran performers chewing up concrete scenery and strutting through a thrilling and wholesome caper. It's a "one last hurrah" type of flick with a niche appeal that lets the ensemble shine. The faux confidence, the spoiled gangsters, the tired seniors who pray that newbies can learn an ounce of respect along the way – it's all so memorably old-fashioned. Even with all that – and as much as you'll laugh – Harry's arc still latches onto your soul in a pure and special way. That's the power of Turturro, but kudos also go to Segan's rich idiosyncrasies that draw us into Harry's gravitational pull.

articles.title: Zendaya's Chani Is the X-Factor That Makes Dune: Part Three So Exciting
articles.summary: The Dune: Part Three trailers remind us that Zendaya's Chani is the critical X-factor that makes this latest sequel so exciting.
articles.body:
With another trailer for Dune: Part Three arriving, we continue to notice how Part Three is not goinig to be a straightforward adaptation of 1969’s Dune Messiah. The story is moving in a very different direction in the third and final part of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy, and we couldn’t be more excited.

What makes this adaptation so different from the source material? It all has to do with Zendaya’s Chani, a character who looks to be playing a profoundly different role in this version of the Dune mythos. Let’s explore what’s changed and why Chani is the secret X-factor that’s transforming this iconic sci-fi saga.

Warning: This article contains spoilers for the Dune novels!

Chani’s Fate: The Dune Books vs. the Movies

2024’s Dune: Part Two already strongly hinted that Villeneuve was taking Chani’s story in a very different direction. In general, Chani is a much more passive character in Frank Herbert’s Dune novels. After being trained in the Atreides brand of combat (known as the weirding way), Chani mostly settles into her role as Paul’s lover and concubine. She stands back as Paul steps onto the Imperial throne and ushers in a cosmic jihad that kills billions.

In Dune Messiah, Chani remains a quiet but fierce supporter of her lover’s cause. She wants nothing more than to bear Paul’s children. Unfortunately for her, Chani is being secretly fed contraceptives by Paul’s wife, Irulan, as the Bene Gesserit have no desire to see their centuries-old breeding program upset by the addition of a random Fremen woman. Paul knows of Irulan’s actions. However, he foresees that the birth of a child will lead to Chani’s death, so he chooses not to act.

It’s only after Chani switches to a traditional, untainted Fremen diet that she finally becomes pregnant. Unfortunately, again, her years of exposure to Irulan’s contraceptives have left her body ill-equipped to deal with the strain of pregnancy. Chani ultimately dies in childbirth, leaving Paul one final surprise when he realizes that she was pregnant with twins.

Dune: Part Two doesn’t do anything to tee up that storyline for Chani in the sequel. Quite the opposite. Zendaya’s Chani is shown to be a much more active participant in Timothée Chalamet’s Paul’s war against the Harkonnens. But unlike Javier Bardem’s Stilgar and his band of religious fanatics, Chani doesn’t buy into the idea of Paul being a prophesied messiah. She sees through the deceptions and stories planted by the Bene Gesserit. She follows Paul because he seeks to fight alongside the Fremen and liberate Arrakis, not to take power for himself.

That all changes at the end of the film, when Paul crowns himself Emperor and takes Florence Pugh’s Irulan as his wife. Chani sees this as a deeply personal betrayal and a rejection of everything Paul claimed to stand for. She has no interest in being part of Paul’s holy war, so Chani retreats back to the desert. Paul wins his war, but in the process, he makes himself totally alone.

Again, everything we’ve seen of Dune: Part Three so far suggests Chani is playing a vastly different role compared to the source material. Her status quo is completely different. She isn’t Paul’s faithful concubine, pining for the day she can proudly bear his children. She’s rejected Paul and everything he stands for, preferring instead to live as a true Fremen, totally free and a servant to no one.

At this point, we can only guess as to the role Chani will play in Dune: Part Three. The marketing is certainly playing up the tragedy of her doomed romance with Paul. The film’s new poster highlights their growing rivalry, making it appear as though Paul and Chani will be forced to battle one another in the desert. The original teaser trailer features what appears to be a scene set during the events of Part Two, as Paul and Chani reflect on the names they want for their future children. The second trailer, meanwhile, shows us what is likely a flashback scene set just after Part Two, as Paul confronts an angry, disillusioned Chani and is accused of seizing undeserved power.

“At the end of the second film, Chani is obviously feeling a sense of betrayal toward Paul, and their relationship has crumbled,” Chalamet said at the fan event where the second trailer was screened . “Without giving too much away, in the third film I think it’s sort of Denis weaving in storylines that weren’t explicit in the book. Perhaps, I would say that’s where Denis took the most creative liberty, but it really ties the story together. Zendaya, as you guys see in that trailer, gives such a fantastic performance in this, as usual.”

For Chalamet, Paul’s fall from grace is a critical part of the Dune storyline, and this revamped approach to Chani feeds into that. It’s not that Paul is a villain, per se. He’s a man trapped by his visions of the future and trying to navigate the best path forward for his family and humanity at large.

“I hope it’s more nuanced than that,” Chalamet said. “I think it’s one of the great endings of Frank Herbert’s books. I think I read somewhere that it’s why he wrote Messiah as a follow-up to the first book, that people mistook Paul as a classic hero. He sort of wanted to warn the world what can happen when people blindly follow leaders, and that even the good can be corrupted.”

The real question is just how far Chani will go to oppose Paul now. Is she simply exiled in the desert, or is she actively resisting his regime? She won’t be the only Fremen who’s lost faith in Paul. Part Three also introduces a character named Farok (Isaach de Bankolé), one of Paul’s Fedaykin commandos who becomes disillusioned with the Lisan al-Gaib after encountering an ocean for the first time (we see part of that scene in trailers).

Like Dune Messiah, Part Three features an alliance of anti-Atreides power players like Reverend Mother Mohaim (Charlotte Rampling), Irulan (Florence Pugh), and a Tleilaxu named Scytale (Robert Pattinson). One intriguing possibility is that Chani joins this alliance in the film. She would certainly be a powerful ally in the war to unseat the Emperor, but would Chani stoop to colluding with Paul’s enemies in order to stop him?

Either way, many fans are beginning to speculate that Scytale uses Chani’s image against Paul in the film. Scytale is a shape-shifter known as a Face Dancer, meaning he can contort his muscles and take on the appearance of anyone he chooses. Some have pointed out that something seems off about Chani in the scene in the trailers where she taunts Paul, “How does it feel to be human like everyone else, Paul Atreides?” Is this the real Chani, or is it Scytale in disguise?

And then there are Paul and Chani’s children. We know those characters also have a part to play in Dune: Part Three. As mentioned, Leto II and Ghanima are born near the end of Dune Messiah, but they’re simply helpless infants in that story. Their true importance to the Dune saga doesn’t become apparent until the third book, 1976’s Children of Dune, when they replace Paul as the series’ main protagonists.

But here, again, Villeneuve is diverging significantly from the source material. Villeneuve has gone so far as to cast teen actors Nakoa-Wolf Momoa and Ida Brooke as Leto II and Ghanima, respectively. Perhaps the characters will appear only via spice-induced visions (as Anya Taylor-Joy’s Alia did in Dune: Part Two), but we suspect their role is more crucial. Given that Paul and Chani are clearly broken up in Part Three, it’s likely that Chani is already pregnant by the time she leaves Paul’s side. By the main timeline of the film, Paul will already be a father to twin teenagers. In that sense, Part Three may be drawing as much from Children of Dune as it is Dune Messiah.

Much like Chani’s rejection of Team Paul, the existence of these Atreides children changes everything for the film. It raises all manner of interesting questions. Is Chani raising the children herself? Is she teaching them to reject Paul’s jihad? How will the Fremen react to the discovery that Muad’Dib has two heirs? Perhaps most importantly, does Paul himself know about his children? Given his supernatural powers, we would imagine so, but he may also be keeping that information close to the stillsuit, out of a desire to protect his family from their many enemies.

It is worth reiterating that, in the book, Paul is surprised to discover Chani has given birth to twins rather than a single daughter. That’s because Leto II is born with prescience, making him invisible to Paul’s oracular sight. This could also play into their role in the film, if Leto II’s very existence shields him and his family from their father’s all-seeing gaze.

Leto II doesn’t appear in the trailers as far as we can tell, but there may be a couple of brief shots of Ghanima. Honestly, Brooke looks so much like Zendaya that it’s hard to be sure. But despite the deceptive editing, that does appear to be Ghanima who stops the charging Sandworm in its tracks near the end of the second trailer. It’s a sign that she, like her brother, has powerful abilities that promise to change the playing field in Dune: Part Three.

The first two films in the series were great, but they didn’t necessarily hold many surprises for fans of the Dune books. This time around, Chani and her children have the potential to completely shake up a familiar story and keep even the most hardcore Dune-heads on their toes. That’s why this latest sequel is so exciting.

For more on Dune: Part Three, learn who’s who in the first teaser trailer .

Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky .

articles.body:
Check out the Carrie Season Two announcement video as the horror series from showrunner Mike Flanagan gets renewed for a second season. Carrie stars Summer H. Howell as Carrie White and Samantha Sloyan as Margaret White.

The series sees Mike Flanagan again at the helm as showrunner and executive producer, alongside returning executive producer Stephen King, as they bring the next chapter of the story to life in Season Two.

From visionary showrunner Mike Flanagan, the urgent and unexpected reimagining of Stephen King’s seminal story brings new depth and complexity to its iconic characters, exploring the forces that shape Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) as she navigates the cruelty and pressures of the modern world. But Carrie’s story doesn’t stop at Prom – it’s far from over…much remains in store from Mike Flanagan and Stephen King, as new revelations will come to light, major character arcs, and plenty of shocking twists.

All eight episodes of Season One of Carrie are available now on Prime Video.

articles.title: Valve Developer Mistakenly Mentions Rumored Half-Life 3 Codename
articles.summary: A Valve developer mistakenly slipped up and made mention of Half-Life 3's long rumored codename during a recent conference.
articles.body:
A Valve developer mistakenly slipped up and made mention of Half-Life 3's long-rumored codename during a recent conference.

For years, fans have wondered if we'll ever see Half-Life 3. During the 2010s, hope for the threequel was kept firmly alive by die-hard fans... but it was later revealed that the project had been quietly killed by Valve. However, hope was reignited when Valve released Half-Life: Alyx, which ended with a massive cliffhanger that seemed to directly set up Gordon Freeman's next adventure. Ever since then, there have been rumors of a third game, with various dataminers discovering references to a project known as "HLX" in various Valve-related files. It has been believed for years that HLX is indeed Half-Life 3, as no one has been able to link it to any other existing Valve project. (And, of course, the acronym all but screaming that it's Half-Life related.)

Now, Valve has acknowleged the project itself, though not on purpose. During a recent Q&A panel at GameSoundCon, a conference for video game audio, Valve's music designer, Mike Morasky, was explaining how the developer handled certain sound systems and noted that Deadlock uses a particular type of high dynamic range audio... and HLX uses its own kind of HDR.

We have the first mention of HLX by a Valve employee. HLX files today. I'm working as quickly as I can. — Tyler "Hype Merchant" McVicker (@Tyler_McV) October 22, 2026

We have the first mention of HLX by a Valve employee. HLX files today. I'm working as quickly as I can.

Once the words HLX came out of Morasky's mouth, he pretty much stopped talking. Whether that's because he had finished his thought or if he realized he should stop talking is up in the air. A colleague sitting next to Morasky then quietly said "nice work," which some fans have read into as a passive-agressive retort to Morasky's slip up. Fans went buckwild with this small, but notable mistake. Some ran with it, feeling like all of their theories and copium has been vindicated after this mention.

Regardless, this does seem to confirm that HLX is a project that is still actively in development at Valve. We can only hope that it is the long-rumored Half-Life 3, but who knows how far away it could be from being announced, let alone released. Half-Life: Alyx had an exceptionally fast turn around time for being announced and released, so it's possible that a similar pattern would emerge here. If that's the case, maybe we can hope to see it at The Game Awards, but that's still probably a longshot.

articles.title: Saber Interactive CEO Says Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival is Performing 'Extremely Well on PC and Consoles' with More to Come
articles.summary: Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival has been a smash hit, says Saber Interactive CEO Matthew Karch in a post on LinkedIn, and it’s the first of a "series" of releases from the studio that will improve its methodology.
articles.body:
Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival has been a smash hit, says Saber Interactive CEO Matthew Karch in a post on LinkedIn, and it’s the first of a “series” of releases from the studio that will improve how it makes games in the future.

Hellraiser: Revival has proven to be a smashing success, in spite of — or, perhaps because of — its super-spicy content. The game doesn’t skirt around the sex, blood, and gore that defined the source material, causing some content creators to get permanently banned despite taking pains to censor their playthroughs.

In an October 19 LinkedIn post, Saber Interactive CEO Matthew Karch praised the Hellraiser development team, revealing the title has been performing “extremely well on PC and console” since its October 8 release.

He also speculated that AAA titles with massive budgets and lengthy development timelines won’t be sustainable in the industry for much longer (if, indeed, they are right now), instead positing that AA games based on established IPs with smaller budgets are likely a more realistic path forward.

“The game is testament to the notion that an established IP and solid AA development with controlled costs can produce great results and high user scores,” he wrote. “I believe a greater focus on these middle-market IP-driven products, rather than AAA behemoths, is the future to maintaining growth and momentum in the game industry.

“While I believe there will always be a place for the properly-developed and budgeted AAA experience, a AA game that provides a great immersive experience for a lower price is less risky and can provide much greater returns on average.”

Karch went on to say that Hellraiser: Revival is “the first in a series of releases by Saber that will continue to prove out our methodology,” teasing that there’s “more to come in just a few short weeks.”

While IGN scored the game a six out of ten , Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival boasts a “very positive” player score on Steam , and has earned no small amount of praise from content creators who showed up in droves to broadcast the game on release.

Of course, given its content, it’s no surprise that some streamers got the ban hammer — but, according to its developers, that’s exactly what they were aiming for when they made it.

"It was an unofficial goal of the team to be banned, unrated, or restricted at least somewhere in the world as one barometer of whether we’d done our jobs right,” narrative director Antony De Fault told IGN in an exclusive interview .

Even Clive Barker himself was impressed , saying he was “fearful at one point that the game would be overly censored but I’m genuinely astonished by how far they’ve been able to push it.”

articles.title: Cyberpunk 2 Associate Director Says Half of Game's Quest Team Are Former Modders
articles.summary: Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Pawel Sasko revealed that much of the game’s staff are actually former modders who CD Projekt Red picked up to work on the highly-anticipated sequel.
articles.body:
Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Pawel Sasko revealed that a good chunk of the game’s staff are actually former modders who CD Projekt Red picked up to work on the highly-anticipated sequel.

Sasko made these comments during one of CDPR’s REDstreams on October 21, where the team discussed the bevy of exciting new updates coming to Cyberpunk 2077 . As part of this discussion, they explained their decision to introduce cross-platform support for PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch 2, and Xbox Series X|S, saying this was done both to keep the game fresh and to actively support the creativity of its modders.

In fact, the good folks at CDPR have actually partnered with modders in the game’s community as part of these updates, and even credited them with helping keep the title afloat.

“The modding community is really keeping the game alive,” Sasko said. “I’m very often looking at what our modders are doing, what they’re building. It’s very exciting. There’s so much creativity. We as a studio always try to support our modding community as much as we can.”

Adding onto this discussion, Sasko revealed that CDPR has sourced quite a few of its staff working on Cyberpunk 2 from the game’s modding scene, saying that around half of its quest team — designers who create a game’s objectives and storyline segments — are former modders.

"A lot of modders, they were players who actually first played and actually got experience with customizing the game with the mods," he said. "For me, this is a foot-in-the-door technique, and a gateway into game dev," he continues. "You can see, and you can learn how things are made, how things can be built. We actually hired so many modders. I would say, at this point, half of the quest team is all former modders."

While this isn’t a completely new revelation as far as CDPR is concerned (Sasko actually revealed this information back in 2024 ), it certainly couldn’t come at a funnier time, given the ongoing discussion around the differing sentiments toward community patches, mods, and emulation happening between Western players and Japanese fans on social media right now .

It’s an exciting era for Cyberpunk chooms; Edgerunners 2 just released on Netflix to rave reviews, alongside a host of new additions to the actual game, which include a dual-wielding playstyle, fresh cyberware customization options, and even a mode that gives you a tour through Night City, on top of cute references to the anime spinoff.

You can read our review for Edgerunners 2 here , as well as our interviews with producer Bartozs Szytbor, who told us all about Roman’s backstory and why the show’s ending wasn’t what audiences anticipated .

articles.title: The next-gen Xbox won’t cost you $1,800. It can’t. Can it?
articles.summary: After a report that Microsoft’s Xbox Helix might cost $1,800, The Verge explores the possibilities.
articles.body: Fortune dropped a bombshell report on the future of gaming this week. According to the publication’s Microsoft insiders, the next Xbox is projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 when it arrives in 2028. My first reaction: The next Xbox is dead on arrival. It’s DOA. My second thought: Microsoft knows people won’t pay that much. It couldn’t possibly charge that much money if it wants next gen to be a success. “I wouldn’t release it at all,” former Microsoft exec Mike Ybarra recently said. My third thought: Didn’t Microsoft already say out loud that it knows people won’t pay that much? * Didn’t old Xbox boss Phil Spencer say “We’re not going to grow the market with $1,000 consoles”? * Didn’t new Xbox boss Asha Sharma say “We’ve reached a point where it will be hard to imagine that mass audiences can afford thousands of dollars to spend” on a box? * Didn’t Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball say the entire company would change its practices to make sure it’s affordable? * Didn’t Sharma say Xbox would need to adopt “radically different business models” to keep Xbox from being too pricey? Did Fortune get it wrong? I don’t think Fortune’s insiders are the problem here. With today’s incredibly overpriced RAM and storage, it wouldn’t be surprising if it cost over a thousand dollars to build, package, distribute, and sell “the largest technical leap you will have ever seen in a hardware generation,” as former Xbox president Sarah Bond called the next Xbox back in 2024. But there are at least five ways the report could be correct without making you pay all that money at once. I just don’t think you’re going to like most of them. Subsidies: Microsoft could pay to give you a discount The least-likely possibility is the one Fortune suggests itself. Let’s look at the original quote, bolding mine: > […] the price of the Helix console has internally been projected to cost consumers between $1,200 and $1,800, unless Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost. Historically, Microsoft has subsidized the Xbox. Microsoft sold boxes at a loss right out of the gate, making its profits when you buy games and Xbox Game Pass subscriptions instead of on the hardware alone. That’s not our speculation — it’s exactly what Microsoft told The Verge in 2021. In 2023, we learned that Microsoft may have spent $1.5 billion to make sure it could sell the Xbox Series X and S at $499 and $299 respectively, instead of what they actually cost. But Microsoft has suggested that it’s done with hardware subsidies. “Going forward, this cannot continue,” wrote Sharma in her “Xbox reset” memo, referring to the $20 billion in content, platform, and hardware subsidies Microsoft made over the past five years. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella echoed that idea on the Hard Fork podcast: “No one can accuse Microsoft of not having invested for the last 25 years, and now we have to turn this into a sustainable business.” It isn’t just new management that’s hinting at no more subsidies: Bond primed the pump for a $1,000 box when she called Helix “a very premium, very high-end curated experience” late last year, comparing it to gaming PCs like the $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld. Perhaps Microsoft has changed its mind since then. “We are working very hard to rethink everything that we can about Helix,” Ball said in June, referring to affordability. “The plan’s the plan until it’s not the plan,” Sharma said in February (though not about affordability specifically). But subsidies would be a tremendous risk if the Helix still plays PC games in addition to Xbox ones. Valve’s Steam is by far the dominant PC gaming platform — so PC gamers who buy a Helix won’t help Microsoft recoup its money. Subscription: “Get it free with 36 months of Xbox Game Pass and qualifying trade-in” There’s another way Microsoft could subsidize a $1,200 Xbox. Today, AT&T will give you a $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro for $0* — if you lock yourself into 36 months of AT&T phone service that costs $100 or more per month and trade in a recent phone, too. Microsoft could do the same with a new, pricier tier of its Xbox Game Pass game subscription service, effectively bundling the games with the console and making you slowly pay for both at the same time. Perhaps you’ll have the option to buy an “unlocked” Xbox for full price, but it won’t be the norm. To make it happen directly, Microsoft would need a pricier new tier of Xbox Game Pass, which wouldn’t necessarily align with the company’s recent moves. Sharma actually cut the price of Game Pass Ultimate to $22.99 a month in April, writing that “Game Pass has become too expensive for players,” while removing Call of Duty games and unlimited access to Xbox Cloud Gaming from the deal. I don’t know if it would work. People feel naked leaving the house without phone service. They might not feel the same about games. Subscription fatigue is real. But if it worked, Microsoft’s moat would be stronger than ever. You’ll be more likely to play the games you’ve already paid for and are committed to keep paying for. Many would get sucked into a profitable upgrade cycle, just like they do with phones, since they can buy the next Xbox for “$0” as soon as it comes out. Cellphone subsidies have been around nearly as long as pricey phones: The 1994 IBM Simon, arguably the first smartphone, eventually cost half its $1,100 price tag if you signed a contract with BellSouth. My first phone, a Kyocera QCP-6035 with a built-in PalmPilot, was subsidized when it arrived in 2001. So it’s not exactly a “radical new business model,” but it would be new for game consoles. Rental: Maybe most people won’t own a Helix themselves It’s also possible that Microsoft simply doesn’t plan to sell a console to the masses anymore — it can sell an $1,800 Xbox to those who can afford “video game ownership” and try to hook everyone else on the Netflix model. After all, the “K-shaped economy” and RAMageddon have already made gaming PCs and existing game consoles into luxury goods. Society’s wealthier individuals seem perfectly happy to pay inflated prices for the few consoles Sony and Microsoft still pump out. While PS5 sales plummeted after Sony’s price hikes, that may have been about component shortages rather than decreased demand. Xbox sales reportedly rose over a similar period, and Microsoft has justified repeated, dramatic price hikes on its consoles since May 2025. “I can tell you definitively, demand for our console exceeds supply. We are putting them in as many stores as possible, we are producing them as quickly as possible. There is a severe limitation to how quickly we can do that,” Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball told The Game Business in June, blaming RAM shortages. But Microsoft has another way of giving less affluent people access to “next-gen” Xbox power. It can rent you one. The company just launched pay-as-you-go cloud gaming starting at $3.99 for 10 hours of cloud gaming (50 hours for $11.99). Maybe all of Microsoft’s recent talk about affordability isn’t about the masses owning a next-gen console. Maybe it’s about finding an affordable way for people to “play Xbox” without owning the games at all. The next gen is the current gen After Fortune’s report, some of the very first reactions I saw boiled down to this: “I’m out. Forget next gen, I’m going to stick with my existing Xbox/PlayStation/Switch.” That’ll be the reality for many people if the Xbox costs over a thousand bucks. But if the RAM shortage continues — if Microsoft knows it’ll sell every Xbox it can make to wealthy individuals because it can’t make a lot — it’s not necessarily a huge risk to sell it sky-high on day one. Perhaps the Xbox Helix will be an early adopter console, the same way the iPhone Duo is an early adopter phone, the same way the Steam Frame is an early adopter headset. These products are selling out instantly despite their high price tags, leaving many would-be buyers in the cold. They’re shipping messy and unfinished, but that’s okay because early adopters want to come along for the ride. Microsoft knows the same is true of some Xbox buyers, because it helped ship an unfinished $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld even before the RAM crisis, and the $1,300 Xbox Ally X20 follow-up is already sold out. But if Microsoft splits the Xbox audience into “have” and “have-not,” it means the next generation won’t truly arrive. Game developers won’t spend all their effort targeting a console people can’t buy. The next Xbox won’t be any more necessary than a PS5 Pro if you already own a PS5. In industry lingo, the Helix would be a “mid-cycle refresh” instead of true next gen. I wouldn’t hate that, though, and neither would many video game execs. They’ve long complained that the pace of technology has ballooned the cost of building a video game to unsustainable levels, leading to today’s world where too many development teams are cut to the bone right after their games ship. Former PlayStation and Xbox execs like Shuhei Yoshida, Shawn Layden, and Mike Ybarra have argued that the next gen isn’t necessary. “Stick with PS5 Pro/Series X until prices normalize. The capabilities of those boxes are both fine for 99% of the audience. No one is screaming ‘I need a more powerful console’ right now,” Ybarra tweeted on October 20th. “I think [Sony and Nintendo] should try to keep the current generation as long as possible, because I think people are very happy using PS5 and Switch 2,” Yoshida told me on The Vergecast. “I think we’ve plateaued on the tech, frankly,” Layden told GamesIndustry.biz in 2025. (He’s said similar before and since.) “Make it cheaper and simpler. Let’s do that instead. And let’s find a way to have more hardware companies participate.” Microsoft and its chip partner AMD have already taken one step to help extend the current generation — AMD’s performance-enhancing FSR 4.1 is coming to Xbox Series S and X, which should make it easier for both to deliver crisp 4K images to your TV. Pay what you can afford Even if Microsoft ships a $1,800 console, the company’s been clear it won’t be the only Xbox you can buy. Sharma has publicly said that Helix will be a “family of devices,” which has been broadly interpreted to mean that Microsoft will let PC industry partners like Asus sell their own “Xbox” as well. If the reporting pans out, that wouldn’t just be a cobranded Xbox Ally handheld that runs Windows — Asus could make a console-shaped box that runs a Windows-based Xbox OS, too. Some of those partners could offer more affordable, less powerful Xboxes than Microsoft’s own flagship box, perhaps with less storage and memory. Microsoft, too, might have creative solutions for storage, like how the company shipped the Xbox 360 with different-size hard drives, or none at all, to make it more affordable. “We will have to empower customers to have very flexible storage offerings,” Sharma said in June. Or you could buy another Xbox that’s likely going to continue to count as part of Microsoft’s “family”: the existing Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S. This can all work because games don’t need to target a single console anymore; they haven’t needed to for a long time. An Xbox One game runs on an Xbox One X and an Xbox Series S and an Xbox Series X because they’re all effectively AMD-powered Windows PCs, just with different amounts of performance on tap. The Xbox Helix is a powerful extension of the same continuum. The same is true of PlayStation 4, PS4 Pro, PS5, PS5 Pro, and presumably PS6, minus the Windows part. Perhaps a particular piece of hardware will stand out as the one developers should target as the baseline for “it looks and runs great on Xbox,” the same way the Steam Deck handheld became a baseline for PC game developers starting in 2022. Maybe, like the Steam Deck and the Nintendo Switch, it’ll help reset our expectations of what a top-shelf game needs to look like. At this rate, I wouldn’t be surprised if the existing Xbox Series S will be the one. But it could also be Microsoft’s own next handheld Xbox. Fortune’s insiders say it’s coming holiday 2027.

articles.title: Call of Duty promises a return to form - but can it compete with GTA?
articles.summary: Modern Warfare 4 faces an uphill battle after last year's Call of Duty missed the mark with fans.
articles.body:
Call of Duty is back - and it's got a lot to prove.

Last year was a low point for the video game juggernaut, with poor reviews for its single-player campaign mode and multiplayer fans defecting to rival titles.

So for latest instalment, Modern Warfare 4, publisher Activision is pulling out all the stops to bring fans back on board.

But with increasing competition for fans' time and attention, and the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 just weeks away, can Call of Duty still cut through?

BBC Newsbeat spoke to some of those behind the game to find out, and why they see the upcoming release of GTA 6 as an "opportunity".

Since 2009, Call of Duty has been at the top - or a close second-place - in the US video game sales charts every year.

But 2025's edition, Black Ops 7, dropped to seventh place in America, according to data from analytics firm Circana. In the UK, it was the eighth best-selling game .

It’s thought the game’s inclusion on Xbox’s Game Pass subscription service, where it won’t appear on release this year, hit sales.

But competition from long-running rival Battlefield 6 and new release Arc Raiders - a surprise success from Swedish studio Embark - put the behemoth on the back foot.

Fans also complained about the inclusion of novelty skins, which change the appearance of characters during multiplayer games, based on cartoons and other pop culture crossovers.

Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, admits it was a tough year for the series.

"I think we missed expectations with our community last year," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

"So we took a step back, we listened to them."

Players now have the ability to switch off controversial cosmetic changes, and Bahl says Modern Warfare 4 is a "return to form".

It's a message they've been keen to get out.

Newsbeat meets Bahl in a corner of Shoreditch, London, that's been turned into a convincing replica of a South Korean street complete with noodle bars and convenience stores.

A similar installation to promote Modern Warfare 4 has been built in downtown LA - but it's far from the only extravagant promotional attempt to generate buzz around the game.

Back in July, Activision recruited Obsession star Inde Navaratte - who streamed Call of Duty on Twitch before becoming one of Hollywood's hottest young stars - to publicise the game at sports convention Fanatics Fest .

It's also struck a sponsorship deal with six-a-side football championship Baller League and worked with world's biggest YouTuber Mr Beast to showcase the game's new DMZ multiplayer mode .

Bahl says the events and collabs are designed to demonstrate Call of Duty's "stature, swagger and scale" - something he admits does not come cheap.

He says he's always thinking of ways for Call of Duty to leverage its position and "show up in culture in a really big and innovative way" to reach "as many people as possible".

Call of Duty does have some strong competition in that space, however.

This year it's launching just weeks before GTA 6 - arguably the most anticipated video game of the decade.

Despite rising console prices, there's hope that the massive interest in Rockstar Games' ultra-blockbuster will convince people to buy a new console or return to the hobby.

Bahl says GTA 6 and Call of Duty are "the two biggest games of the year" but they're not necessarily in direct competition.

"More people dusting off their Xbox or their PlayStation, starting to play for the first time it gives an opportunity for more gamers to come in and play both of the games," says Bahl.

GTA 6 will only be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles at first, and multiplayer modes won't be available at launch.

"So we feel like this is differentiated enough to really stand out," says Bahl.

The game itself sells for about £70 in the UK, but Bahl points out it can be a year-round hangout space for many fans.

"The number one reason people come to Call of Duty is not just for the combat or the gunplay, but it's actually because their friends are there, right?

"And so that social connection is so powerful."

One of the biggest criticisms of last year's Call of Duty was its single-player campaign mode.

The short, cinematic adventures are rarely the main reason players pick up the latest title, but are nevertheless popular.

Alternating titles in the series follow different storylines, and the Modern Warfare strand has produced some of Call of Duty's most beloved characters.

Activision has said Modern Warfare 4 is the "epic conclusion" to the story of fan favourite Capt John Price, played by British actor Barry Sloane.

"It's a lot of surprises, a culmination of all those pieces that we've been putting together coming together," he says.

Sloane tells Newsbeat he's not too intimidated by the weight of expectation.

"I've been greeted with love from the fan base since the get-go," he says.

María Elisa Camargo, who returns to the series as cartel leader Valeria Garza, admits the fanbase is "a tough crowd".

"They're very smart, very story-driven, and they're not just loving anyone," she says.

Actor Mads Mikkelsen, known for appearances in films such as Casino Royale and TV show Hannibal, plays mysterious enemy The Archer.

He says there's at least one player who'll be there to play through the campaign.

"I know for sure my son will try to kill me again and again.

Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here .

articles.title: Brewers owner takes jab at Dodgers in latest response to Tarik Skubal trade
articles.summary: brewers skubalThe Dodgers won the trade deadline with the acquisition of Tarik Skubal — but that doesn’t mean they ultimately prevailed. The Brewers were rep...
articles.body:
The Dodgers won the trade deadline with the acquisition of Tarik Skubal — but that doesn't mean they ultimately prevailed.

The Brewers were reportedly in the mix to land Skubal in a blockbuster trade, but Milwaukee managed to sweep the Dodgers despite losing out on the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner.

Brewers owner Mark Attanasio discussed the pursuit of Skubal and slipped in a slight jab directed at the Dodgers during an appearance on The Post's "The Show" podcast hosted by Jon Heyman and Joel Sherman.

"This team was built, not bought. It's critical to look at how we got here, and because I want to have sustained success, we had to do that by being careful about how many prospects we gave up," Attanasio said.

"I thought a lot about it. If we had not won that Game 4, we would've seen Skubal and [Yoshinobu Yamamoto] again, and we could've been looking at Game 7."

The 2026 World Series brings an interesting conversation to light as the Brewers and Rays managed to reach baseball's biggest stage as small-market teams.

The Dodgers had the highest payroll of MLB's final four teams, but were eliminated in four games by Milwaukee.

Attanasio's comments ring true, the Brewers have taken years to build a winning team and it appears the squad has a strong chance of hoisting the Commissioner's Trophy. But many of the Dodgers' biggest critics tend to overlook the team's top farm system.

While money is no object for the Dodgers, the team wouldn't have won back-to-back World Series if the organization didn't have the ability to make blockbuster trades because of its top prospects.

Skubal didn't guarantee the Dodgers another ring, but it certainly improved their chances.

Where the Dodgers go this winter will likely determine how long the dynasty lasts for LA.

articles.title: Dustin May's Last Outing Should Give Brewers Some Confidence For World Series
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers have gone with a bullpen game once in each round of the postseason
articles.body:
There are not many holes or flaws on this year's Milwaukee Brewers.

The biggest questions coming into the postseason were whether they could hit for power and whether their rotation was deep enough. Well, they have answered the power question by hitting 10 home runs, more than any team, and the questions about the rotation have not mattered since Robert Gasser and the bullpen have stepped up.

Jacob Misiorowski, Robert Gasser and Logan Henderson will start Games 1, 2 and 3 most likely, and the Brewers will likely throw a bullpen game.

They did so against the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers. In both of those games, Dustin May was the "bulk" guy, even though Aaron Ashby notched a three-inning save in Game 4 against the Dodgers.

Against the Padres, May went three innings, allowing two earned runs and striking out three batters. Against the Dodgers, May went three innings, allowing three earned runs, all of which came on one swing from Shohei Ohtani on a pitch down and in.

After a rough second inning against the Dodgers, in which he also let an inherited runner score, May gave the Brewers something positive to take away from the game. He worked a clean third inning and gave up one single in the fourth inning, but did not allow a run.

He ended his outing with two scoreless frames and looked more like the player the Brewers expected when they traded for him.

May has had a good outing with the Brewers this year, but has been inconsistent overall. When they acquired him, they were expecting to get a clear starter for their postseason rotation. However, his role right now is to go as long as he can, and as soon as the Brewers think his stuff is declining, they pull him.

However, he should still be seen as an option to go multiple innings in Game 4 of the World Series, assuming the Brewers are not down 3-0 and have to get crazy with their pitching plans.

He ended Game 4 on a high note, and if he draws the start in Game 4 of the World Series, he may surprise some fans and go deeper than he has previously. If the Brewers can get five innings out of him, it would be great.

articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays made one of the most impactful moves ahead of the 2026 MLB trade deadline by acquiring Freddy Peralta from the New York Mets. Peralta is now set to play against the team in the World Series that he pitched for before joining the Mets in the Milwaukee Brewers. On Thursday, Peralta revealed his career plans for his future in Tampa Bay with the Rays, via Foul Territory.

"I'm very comfortable here," Peralta said. "I would love to stay here for the rest of my career, especially because there's a lot of people that I love here… They are very smart, they know what they're doing. I know that they are going to help me to get better for the future years. And also, for me, I live in Florida and everything is easier for me in general. Not only in baseball, but in life."

Peralta is set to become a free agent following the 2026 season. It remains to be seen if he will return to Tampa Bay, but his comments suggest he's certainly open to a potential reunion.

Drew Rasmussen will likely get Game 2, meaning Peralta is on track to start Game 3 of the World Series back in Tampa Bay. articles.title: Clayface Ending Explained
articles.summary: The new movie Clayface marks the live-action film debut of the classic Batman villain but fans are obviously wondering if the film also introduces the DCU’s incarnation of the Caped Crusader. We’re gonna dive into how Clayface ends, how the character’s design was created for the film, and yes, the Batman of it all.
articles.body:
Let's make this simple: You want to know if there are any mid- or post-credits scenes in Clayface . The answer is no.

The new movie Clayface marks the live-action film debut of the classic Batman villain but fans are obviously wondering if the film also introduces the DCU’s incarnation of the Caped Crusader. It does not.

We’re gonna dive into how Clayface ends, how the character’s design was created for the film, and yes, the Batman of it all… so read on!

While Batman is never even mentioned here, the movie does feature a scene set at the Wayne Community Centre. But let’s be clear: Batman already exists in Clayface’s Gotham City and in the DCU at large.

Remember, the DCU’s Batman already popped up in animated form for a cameo in Creature Commandos. Matt Hagen’s Clayface also made his animated DCU debut in that show, where he was voiced by Alan Tudyk. (The live-action version of Matt Hagen doesn’t quite jibe with the animated version. Hagen also appeared to have been killed off in Creature Commandos, but DCU Studios co-boss James Gunn later confirmed that Clayface survived .)

Of that version of the Caped Crusader, Gunn already confirmed last year that “this is the DCU Batman ,” but the character was kept in silhouette because he was not yet ready to commit to a final costume design. Gunn said the animated cameo was “just a way to introduce that Batman is a part of this universe, he's an important part of this universe, and he has an impact on it.”

And if there was still any doubt after all that, Clayface director James Watkins told me at the film’s press junket, “I would say Batman exists in this world [of Clayface], but it's just not his story. It's Matt Hagen's story. So, it's just like in Joker . It's a city of several million people, and we're telling one person's story within it.”

So we likely won’t see the DCU’s Batman in live-action until Batman: The Brave and the Bold finally makes it to the screen (unless, of course, Gunn sneaks him into next year’s Man of Tomorrow , but that lineup already seems pretty stacked).

It’s also worth noting the timeline of events so far in the DCU. Both Clayface and Creature Commandos take place before the events of Superman , which is set in 2025. Lanterns only references Batman in its sequences set in 2026, so it’s possible that the DCU’s Batman started operating in Gotham City sometime after 2016 and before 2024.

While there’s no post-credits scene, fans will have to wait until the final scenes of DC Studios’ new movie Clayface to see a comics and cartoon-accurate depiction of the monstrous Batman villain.

After finally attaining his revenge on all those who wronged him – from the mobsters who carved up his face to the money manager who stole his fortune and the best friend who betrayed him – former actor Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) turns his sights on Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie).

Matt fell hard for Caitlyn while she was treating him with her experimental nanobot regenerative process, tech that restored his face but also caused his shape-shifting affliction. Despite being engaged to Gotham Police detective John Borrelli (Max Minghella), Caitlyn also developed feelings for Matt. Ultimately, though, she chose not to betray John and become romantically involved with her patient. Caitlyn comes home to the apartment she shares with John to reveal the truth about Matt’s condition, her role in how it happened, and his involvement in the killings. Then she notices the real John’s corpse lying in the next room, having been slain by Matt, who suggests he could stay in John’s form forever if she wants to be with him.

Matt is clearly off his rocker at this point. Caitlyn grabs the taser from John’s belt and zaps Matt, lighting him up and sending him crashing through the window to the street below. As Matt writhes in pain while electricity surges through his nanobot-infested body, Caitlyn retrieves her tablet computer so she can access the destruct sequence for the nanobots, which would also kill Matt in turn. (It should be noted that electricity is one of Batman's preferred weapons against Clayface in other media.)

Outside, Matt transforms into the giant Clayface form that fans will recognize from the comics and animated series, terrifying Caitlin. Tom’s eyes plead with her, his humanity returning briefly enough for him to beg to die. Caitlyn initiates the self-destruct sequence and watches as Matt melts into puddles that drain into the sewer.

Later, Caitlyn is at her lab where she shares all her materials related to Matt with the police. (How and why she isn’t arrested as an accessory to all the murders or for unlawful human experiments is never addressed.) Walking home, she is unnerved looking at strangers’ faces, haunted by Matt’s ability to become anyone in an instant. She stops to buy a newspaper from a vendor. The front page cover story is about Matt’s downfall and death. A homeless man asks her for some money and does a familiar actorly bow when accepting it, a gesture Caitlyn recognizes as one that Matt once did.

We then follow the homeless man back to his dwelling where, as suspected, he’s revealed to actually be Matt. Caitlyn appears behind him, holding the newspaper. He asks her how the reviews are and she tells me he received rave notices. That’s when we see Matt has created both her form and his own from the pool of clay. He cries out in anguished despair once his romantic fantasy life with Caitlyn physically recedes into his monstrous true form.

How Clayface’s Gruesome Final Form Was Realized

I recently chatted with director James Watkins and stars Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie about what went into the filming of Clayface’s final, comics-accurate form. Watkins said it was a lengthy process to settle on the final look, which was not achieved entirely through CGI alone.

“We went through 13, 14 iterations trying to get that [final form] right,” said Watkins. “I wanted to honor the comics and look at that and have something that was true to that. But at the same time, it's got to play as live-action and real and grounded. But also, I wanted to not lose sight [of Harries]. I remember his eye I was most focused on. Not [to] lose sight of the pain, the heartbreak, the man inside the monster, as it were. And that was really, really important to me from when I first read Mike Flanagan's script, the sort of tragedy of that character and that journey.”

Watkins added, “I don't like horror movies that are just clockwork. I like horror movies where they have an emotional connection or a soul or whatever. And that was something that I was most focused on achieving at the end.”

The director said various things were tried on the set to accomplish that, which were then digitally augmented. Ackie recalled “there was a giant man in a suit … he was like 6’10”” who served as Clayface’s in-person stand-in. Ackie clarified that the man was not in a motion-capture suit but rather one that better resembled the character.

For the final interaction between the fantasy Caityn and Matt, who transforms during it, Ackie revealed “it wasn't actually Tom at that point. So without giving anything away, things happen and then the giant man comes in and then he took over, but we were very excited for the giant man.”

DC Universe: Every Upcoming Movie and TV Show

“That day was a pretty cool day,” Harries recalled about filming that scene. “We've been shooting for maybe six or seven hours and it was near the end of the whole shoot. And Naomi and I had maybe gone a bit – we lost the plot. So then we were very impatient for this guy to come.”

Harries added that “there'll be photos and (behind-the-scenes materials) that will come out at the appropriate time. But it was huge discussions with so many different departments about how you achieve that and where you get to. And I think the thing that I find really interesting about Matt throughout this whole (film) is that … he has no concept of Clayface and he doesn't anticipate where this is going. He's just met somebody who might be able to help him and inadvertently falls in love with this person. He thinks he's on a completely different trajectory to the one he ends up going down.”

Clayface is now playing in theaters. For more coverage, be sure to read IGN’s Clayface review and learn what DC Studios’ Peter Safran said about DC’s next film and television projects .

Jim Vejvoda (he/him) is IGN's Assoc. Director of Entertainment Content.

articles.title: Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember Gets Wuxia… and Let Me Fight a Horrific Spider Thing | IGN Preview
articles.summary: Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember is shaping up to be an interesting sequel that combines elements of Team Ninja’s action game expertise with the Three Kingdoms games’ penchant for strategy.
articles.body:
Visually, Wo Long 2 is a beautiful game.

I love that the combat system encouraged me to be aggressive and chase perfection.

I have a confession to make, friends: I’ve never played the original Wo Long. I know, I know. Dust off your pitchforks, light your torches. I have it coming in the same way that we all do. “How could you, Will? You’re an action game guy!” Listen, I’m of the opinion that Team Ninja is one of the best to ever do it. Maybe even the best . But everybody’s got blind spots. That’s what I told myself as a giant spider thing with weird arms named Wugu who I’m sure would have been easier if I’d played the original smashed me into the ground for the umpteenth time. I was also coming into the fight cold. My demo had been split by an interview with producer Mazakazu Hirayama and development producer Masaaki Yamagiwa. Great for this preview. Bad for me. But the beauty of Team Ninja’s games has always been that they ask you to believe you can make it to the next moment, that you can be perfect for just a few more seconds. You have to believe. And I did.

But before we talk about the end, we have to talk about the beginning. My demo started with a simple objective: retake the demonic island. Sure, man. Why not? As I maneuvered my character down the Red Cliffs, I was stunned by Wo Long’s beauty. Team Ninja’s games have always had a distinct visual style, but if I wasn’t marching off to battle the demonic, I’d have stopped to take in the view. Flowers swaying with the wind, a shadow cast by a wooden fence, a leaf carried gently to the ground by the breeze. Even the ships with their brilliant red sails, afire under the cliff, and the glowing mountain of corruption rising from the ground like a severed fist were beautiful, in their own way. Something to fight for, I guess. But beauty isn’t why I’m here.

Down the Cliffs, onto what remains of the pier. Open a chest for some of the loot Team Ninja has become famous (infamous?) for over the years. Raise a flag for the future and morale. Across a rope attached to a ballista’s arrow, I find my first foes. Regular soldiers. My Gray Iron Dual Chakrams (everything, everything is Xena) make quick work of them. God, it’s good to play an action game where weapons have movelists again. Just have to be careful not to follow those poor fools into the water myself. My character can duel with the best of them, but he can’t swim.

Across the water is where I find my favorite trick of the demo: launching a guy into the air and watching as he falls into the water, then jumping away at the last moment so I don’t take the plunge myself. Every game should have jump cancels. Wo Long 2 understands this. Yes.

A couple of boats (and deaths) later and I am coming to grips with Wo Long 2’s combat, its speed. And it is fast, something Hirayama and Yamagiwa emphasized when I spoke to them.

“We got heavy inspiration, obviously because it's set in China, [from] Chinese martial arts. And for example, if we were to take a game that was based in Japan, like a samurai game, the samurai really focuses on the non-movement as well as when they actually have to move. But when we looked at Chinese martial arts, there's a lot of speed, there's a lot of back and forth, there's a lot of over-the-topness to it. So we definitely got the battle system inspiration from that.” But the battle system also emphasizes aggressive play. “One of the concepts that we have for this game is we got every inspiration from Chinese movies… back and forth attack and defense, like action movies…” the producers told me. “There's going to be really speedy combat and a lot of back and forth, but when you perform attacks in series… it's going to open your options up a little more and you'll be able to do more actions by continuing to attack.”

You can feel it immediately. By continuing to land hits, you build your own Spirit gauge, which you can spend on Martials Arts (insert drum roll), special attacks unique to each of Wo Long 2’s 18 weapons or Wizardry. Bolts of lightning to electrocute the unprepared. Freezing your blade to take out enemies made of fire. It’s in making the choices at the right moments, and being willing to play defense, that Wo Long 2 shines. You could just block, I suppose, or roll away. These are the tools we are used to in the soulslike, and they are the weapons of cowards. But there is no stamina gauge here, nothing to limit the fun or prevent you from being aggressive on the attack and risking parries on defense. Transcendence comes in the moments you see the attack coming, all outlined in a flashing red circle enclosing its occupant like a halo, and rush into it for the deflect. Perhaps you will die. Perhaps you will be glorious. But unless you open yourself to failure, neither option can come to pass. Glory is only possible in vulnerability. No heroes were forged in safety, in the conservative. I know what I would rather be.

Or perhaps I would rather be devious. Could I, I wondered as I squared up against Han Xuan and his minions, win by knocking him into the drink? Why should I play fair? One air combo later, and he was sinking to Davy Jones’. Brilliant. I learn not to play by the rules. I attack massive foes with ballistae from a distance. I send enemies to watery graves. I have come to play and to win.

Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember – October 2026 Screenshots

I advance through armored enemies wielding maces bigger than I am, dodge through the arrows of archers foolish enough to hold their ground. I meet the heroes of the Three Kingdoms, save their soldiers, plant flags to raise morale and to bring me back when I fall to seek revenge against the foes who killed me, now strengthened by my defeat. Tecmo Koei is no stranger to the Three Kingdoms setting, something both Hirayama and Yamagiwa joke about when I speak to them, but for Wo Long 2, the team wanted to combine historical events with the dark fantasy element that defines Wo Long as a series. Creating an original character allowed them to do just that.

“We wanted to kind of have that character interact with these events and in a way it's like you could kind of see the behind the scenes of what was going on if this person were to exist when these events were happening… [We] think fans of… Chinese Three Kingdoms history would enjoy this game because it's based off of true events that happened, but even people that don't know, that aren't too privy to the Three Kingdoms will be able to enjoy the story because of how the main character interacts with these events.”

As I move deeper into the corruption, things get more intense. I fight beings made of fire and freeze my blade to dispatch them. I grapple with foes whose limbs are too long and who can kill me almost immediately. Sometimes I fight. Sometimes I run. Sometimes I manifest the presence of a divine beast, the beautiful phoenix, to aid me, and it carries me through. I upgrade and rework my skills. I begin to understand. And Wo Long teaches me every step of the way, largely through its UI. Whenever I have a question, I look at the options on-screen, and they often lead to answers.

My favorite moment in the demo pits me against Shi Huan. I have little health and no healing items. “I’m dead,” I figure. I’ll die, respawn, and try again. But why not make the most of the attempt? I stayed aggressive, wiping out his mooks and then taking the fight to him. I never let up, only pausing long enough to deflect his Critical Blows (the ones outlined in red), and somehow, I did it. It was immensely satisfying. But I wasn’t done. A few more fire demons (and one 30-minute interview) later, and I was facing off against Wugu again.

I beat him, for the record. It took everything I had: a spell that restored my health, the Divine Beast at my back, and a lot of trial and error and getting smacked into the turf by his weird tentacle arm. But I believed, and eventually I did it.

But I’d only seen a fraction of what Wo Long 2 has to offer. When I spoke to them, Hirayama and Yamagiwa emphasized the open field, a more strategic aspect that can have an impact on the enemy’s morale. “There's a lot of small things that you could do within [the] open field… You could attack a smaller squad of the enemy side, and you could even take over that squad, have their leader join you and become an ally. You could attack the enemy's foodstock and kind of lower their morale. As you play the game, you find all these small things that you could do on the battlefield for you to achieve that ultimate objective, main objective. “Three Kingdom games are famous for the strategic aspect, taking over a certain area from the enemies,” they continued. “There's been a lot of that in a lot of these Three Kingdoms games, and we wanted to combine those two aspects... That's one of the main characteristics of the Wo Long series, the soulslike aspect, tons of dying as well as the strategic taking over areas from the enemy.”

My brief time with Wo Long 2 hadn’t allowed me to experience the open field, but it does give me something to look forward to. Still, I had one more question. One very dumb, very selfish question that anyone who had played a Team Ninja game, whether it was Ninja Gaiden or Rise of the Ronin, might have on their mind.. And I needed an answer: would Wo Long 2 have a weapon that featured an Izuna Drop? Hirayama and Yamagiwa laughed at that one. They hadn’t considered it, they told me, but it was a good idea. So who knows? If it shows up, remember this preview

Either way, Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember is shaping up to be an interesting sequel that combines elements of Team Ninja’s action game expertise with the Three Kingdoms games’ penchant for strategy. But what I liked most about my time with it was that it encouraged me to be aggressive and chase perfection. That’s what the best action games do. Will Wo Long 2 live up to that pedigree? That remains to be seen. But it certainly feels like it’s aiming for the right stuff. And if you can make it through the next few seconds, you can make it through anything.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!
